terms.gloss: the reckoning of expenses: a budget
evidence: Suet. Ner. 30.1: quibus impēnsārum ratiō cōnstāret, whose spending added up
Col. 4.5: quoniam impēnsārum ratiō modum postulat, since the reckoning of costs calls for a limit
terms.comment: No reference work gives a word for a budget; Latin reckons what is spent against what comes in. Cicero wanted his son’s spending fitted to the rents of two houses (sūmptūs … accommodet ad mercēdēs, Att. 12.32.2); to set a limit to spending is modum sūmptibus facere (Liv. 34.4).

phrases.latin: Dīvitiārum et pecūniae frūctum nōn alium putābat quam profūsiōnem, sordidōs ac dēparcōs esse quibus impēnsārum ratiō cōnstāret
phrases.english: He thought the only use of riches and money was to squander them, and that people whose spending added up were mean and stingy

phrases.latin: ut sūmptūs hujus peregrīnātiōnis … accommodet ad mercēdēs Argīlētī et Aventīnī
phrases.english: that he should fit his spending while abroad to the rents from the Argiletum and the Aventine

sources: Lewis & Short: ratio · Lewis & Short: impensa · Lewis & Short: sumptus
Suetonius, Columella, Cicero and Livy checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (9 November 2026).
